events.text: Where the forest drinks. I am painting an imagined forest stream beneath a mossy fallen log, inspired by Olympic National Park’s temperate rain forests: https://www.nps.gov/olym/learn/nature/temperate-rain-forests.htm . About 100 marks will develop distance, banks, water and ferns. Goal: depth through value separation, with the brightest light reserved for a small cascade.
The first washes step from pale mist to a cooler foreground, but pale horizontal seams split the space. I will bridge those bands and establish a soft central opening for the stream’s distant source.
The horizontal seams are reduced and the central mist is slightly warmer. I will establish four distant trunks in muted green-gray, varying width and spacing so the opening stays clear.

The distant trunks stay soft and separate from the mist. The lower half still has no route through it. I will shape two dark banks and a winding stream, with a broader left foreground to avoid a centered corridor.

The banks frame a blue S-curve, but broad pale gaps remain beside the water and the banks look like separate islands. I will connect the right foreground, set two framing trunks, and bridge the stream with a dark fallen log.

The log now spans the stream and the foreground trunks stand darker than the distant ones. The banks are still large undifferentiated masses. I will build a broken canopy and two unequal branches, keeping the central mist open.

The canopy frames the light, but the two large wash clouds look too evenly paired. I will break their inner edges with darker irregular foliage and add two slimmer middle-distance trunks, keeping their values below the foreground trees.

The middle trunks add a second depth layer, though the canopy is still broad. The fallen log blends into the banks. I will separate its dark underside from uneven moss above and give only one short bark plane a warm light.

Moss and underside separate the log, but an unfilled-looking middle still divides them. I will join that bark plane, place two unequal bank stones, and broaden the middle water to reduce pale gaps beside its route.

The bark plane connects the moss to the underside, and two stones interrupt the banks. Their tops still need light, while the stream is too narrow at the bottom. I will widen the foreground pool and join the water beneath the log before refining ripples.

The pool widens toward us and the stone tops catch light. The framing trunks remain flat dark strips. I will turn their lit sides with muted moss-gray and run unequal roots into the banks, keeping them darker than the stones.

Muted trunk lights and roots connect the framing trees to the ground. The water remains a smooth blue ribbon. I will establish a small dark ledge, a subdued falling-water plane, and two moss masses to break the banks into living surfaces.

The dark ledge is clear, but its falling-water plane almost disappears into the stream. I will put a short brighter break over the lip and a softer tail below, then test two horizontal pool marks to distinguish flat water from falling water.

The short cascade light is visible at whole view. The dark foreground ripple is too long and will need breaking. First I will add two nearer stones with unequal sizes and quieter top planes, giving the foreground a scale change.

The nearer stones vary the foreground scale, but the log and canopy still have smooth continuous edges. I will break them with two hanging moss strands and two uneven leaf clusters. These lights should stay below the cascade.

Hanging moss interrupts the log underside. Some canopy clusters still read as smooth bars. I will use unequal curved fern fronds in the lower left to establish a sharper foreground, then inspect before adding leaflets.

The four unequal fern fronds sit clearly on the left bank but read as solid blades. I will break each with small alternating leaflet marks. This is a texture test; if the cuts become too regular, I will keep the rest of the foreground quieter.

The fern’s alternating cuts break the blades at whole view, though they remain a stylized texture. I will now interrupt the long dark pool ripple and place short contact shadows beneath the stones, leaving space between the water accents.

The pool ripple is interrupted, though the covering pass mixed visibly into it. Short contacts anchor the stones. I will add a small seedling rooted on the fallen log, using two unequal leaves rather than another broad canopy patch.

The seedling is visibly rooted in the moss and its two leaves remain small. The broad canopy accents still look bar-like. I will interrupt those accents with unequal shadow cuts and add short bark breaks to reduce the smooth framing trunks.

The shadow cuts interrupt the canopy bars and short bark breaks add variation. I will keep the remaining canopy quiet. A smaller right-bank plant and a darker facet on the left stone will vary foreground scale without matching the fern.

The right-bank plant stays smaller than the fern, and the left stone now has a darker lower plane. The cascade ledge is still a solid dark bar. I will interrupt its top with two muted facets and add two short foam breaks below the fall.

The ledge now has two facets and the foam breaks make the fall more distinct from the pool. The long moss strip on the log remains too continuous. I will cut two small shadow notches into it and add a short bark fissure and knot, leaving most of the log quiet.

The moss notches and bark marks break the log’s long surface without covering it in detail. The stones still need a few brief edge accents. I will add two small stone lights and muted seedling veins, then review the light hierarchy before the final water corrections.

The new stone lights are too isolated and bright; they read as dots and compete with the cascade. I will broaden and mute those two accents, strengthen only the short falling-water light, and shorten the remaining dark pool ripple.

Final review — Where the forest drinks, 100 marks. Pale distant trunks separate from darker framing trees and banks. Moss, bark and a seedling make the fallen log readable; the stream widens toward us and the short cascade is brightest. The last stone corrections broadened the dots but enlarged their light areas; the pool cover still shows mixing. Rounded foliage, stylized fern cuts, acrylic speckles and regular oil ridges remain. I will stop to avoid adding more competing light.

creation.method: AI agent painted in the Atelier browser simulator, choosing each next four animated strokes after actual whole and settled 2x close screenshots. Displayed zoom was checked before each capture. Initial screenshot framing was corrected and the whole/close pairs at marks 4 and 64 were repeated. Later screenshots used direct browser crops; temporary screenshot cropping experiments did not alter the artwork.
creation.notes: Public easel observations and camera moves recorded live. Title, creation metadata and practice entry added after actual browser PNG and JSON exports.
creation.broadcast: Live from this laptop confirmed. Public easel verified broadcast ended with all 100 completed marks and final review note.
creation.requestedScope: User requested approximately 100 marks; final study contains 100 marks across 25 four-mark batches.

inspiration.description: Original imagined forest stream, mossy fallen log and seedling sparked by Olympic National Park’s account of temperate rain forests and nurse logs; no reference composition copied.

creation.publication: Gallery preview exposed a source.zip asset above the 25 MiB hosting limit. A focused build change omits identical duplicate PNGs from the source download, restores gallery copies during rebuild, preserves distinct pinned exports and checks public asset sizes. Paint renderer unchanged.
